primitives.name: Risk Aversion Bias
primitives.verbatim_quote: Mangoldt both observed, most men have an irrationally high confidence in their own good fortune, and that this is doubly true when their personal prowess comes into the reckoning, when they are betting on themselves.
primitives.assumptions: Agents exhibit overconfidence in self-reliance under uncertainty.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When personal stakes exceed external validation thresholds.

layer2.mapping: Confidence-weighted utility maximization in subjective risk models.
layer2.telemetry: Overconfidence index vs. actual outcome variance.

primitives.name: Competitive Pressure
primitives.verbatim_quote: To these considerations must be added the stimulus of the competitive situation, constantly exerting pressure to outbid one's rivals, as in an auction sale, where things often bring more than any one thinks they are worth.
primitives.assumptions: Market participants bid beyond intrinsic value due to rivalry.
primitives.breakdown_regime: At equilibrium points where bids exceed marginal utility.

layer2.mapping: Auction-based bidding dynamics mirror profit-setting behavior.

primitives.name: Tenacious Commitment
primitives.verbatim_quote: Men may possibly be timid and critical on first embarking in new ventures, but once committed, it seems unquestionable that the general rule is to hold on to the last ditch, and the greater part of the bidders for productive services are owners of businesses already established.
primitives.assumptions: Once invested, agents resist exit even under negative feedback.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Post-investment phase with diminishing marginal returns.

layer2.telemetry: Exit probability vs. time since investment initiation.

The three core primitives—risk aversion bias, competitive pressure, and tenacious commitment—form a triadic system governing entrepreneurial decision-making. Risk aversion bias introduces cognitive distortion through overconfidence, especially when personal stakes are involved. Competitive pressure amplifies this distortion via auction-like dynamics, pushing valuations above fundamental worth. Tenacious commitment then sustains these distorted decisions post-investment, creating a feedback loop of irrational persistence. These elements together define a non-linear, bounded-rational decision manifold where profit emerges not from accurate valuation but from systemic misalignment between perception and reality. The failure mode occurs when all three interact without corrective mechanisms, leading to speculative bubbles or sustained losses. This framework aligns with behavioral economics and game theory, modeling how bounded rationality and social incentives shape economic outcomes.
